passage: The lift doors were closing when the director asked, "Who came up with the churn analysis?" Nikita opened her mouth. Tanuja had built the model over two weekends, and Nikita had only made the slides. For a second the word "I" sat ready on her tongue, because promotion talks were next month. "Tanuja built the model. I turned it into slides," she said instead, holding the door. The director looked at them both. "Good. Put both names on the summary." Nikita's heart was pounding, half regret and half relief. In the lift she told herself it had cost her nothing yet, and knew that was not quite true.

qa.q: Who built the churn analysis model?
qa.a: Tanuja built the model over two weekends.

qa.q: What was Nikita tempted to do, and what was on her mind?
qa.a: She felt torn, tempted to say "I" and take the credit because promotion talks were next month.

qa.q: Why does naming who did what matter for the team later?
qa.a: It builds trust, and the director asked for both names on the summary, so both people are recognised. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt hearing Nikita's answer?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt relieved and valued, since the real work was named instead of being passed off.

grounding: A colleague is tempted to present shared work as her own but names who did what.

passage:
Akash was stuck in a flooded underpass on his way in, and the regional director had arrived a day early. "Mohit, walk me through the vendor savings," she said, sitting down.
Mohit opened the deck they had built together. The best idea in it, renegotiating the transport contract, was Akash's. The director didn't know that. Akash wasn't there. And the promotion list was being drafted next month.
"I built most of this," Mohit heard himself begin. Then he stopped. It wasn't true, and he would have to look at Akash tomorrow.
He started again. "Akash and I built this together. The transport renegotiation was his idea; he made the calls. I did the numbers on the packaging side."
The director made a note. "Tell Akash I want to talk to him about the transport piece."
At noon Akash arrived, soaked. "How did it go?"
"She wants to talk to you," Mohit said. "It was your idea."

qa.a: He was stuck in a flooded underpass.

qa.q: Why did Mohit begin with "I built most of this"?
qa.a: He felt tempted by the coming promotion list and the chance to look good while Akash was absent.

qa.q: What made Mohit change course, and why was it right?
qa.a: He knew it wasn't true and that he would have to face Akash; naming who did what gave Akash his due and built trust.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when Mohit says "It was your idea"?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, and more trusting of Mohit.

grounding: Shows the temptation to present shared work as one's own and choosing instead to name who did what.

passage:
At the agency in Lower Parel, the campaign line that won the pitch, "Small steps, big city", had come out of a late-night chat between Samir and Baljeet. When the creative head asked at the celebration meeting, "Whose line was that?", Samir said, "Mine," and everyone clapped.
He told himself it was fine. Baljeet was a designer, not a writer. The phrasing was mostly his. He'd have thought of it eventually.
Baljeet said nothing. But for two weeks he stopped staying late, stopped sending sketches after hours, and ate lunch with the design team instead.
Samir felt the change like a draught. One evening he scrolled back through their chat. There it was, in Baljeet's message: "small steps, big city?" Samir had only added the capital letters.
The next morning he went to the creative head. "I need to correct something. The line was Baljeet's. I shouldn't have taken it." Then he found Baljeet at the design desk and said the same, without excuses. Baljeet nodded slowly. "Took you long enough."

qa.q: How did Samir feel after taking the credit, and how did he justify it?
qa.a: He rationalised that Baljeet was a designer and the phrasing was mostly his; underneath, he felt uneasy, noticing the change "like a draught".

qa.q: How did Samir repair the damage?
qa.a: He told the creative head the line was Baljeet's and apologised to Baljeet directly, without excuses.

qa.q: How did Baljeet respond to losing the credit?
qa.a: He quietly withdrew, no longer staying late or sending sketches, and ate lunch with the design team.

grounding: Illustrates taking credit for shared work and rationalising it, then naming who did what because trust matters more.
